prompt: Why does the whole course work on one business's data rather than a fresh example in each lesson?
hint: Think about lesson 5, lesson 10 and lesson 16.

choices.text: So one number can be computed three ways and compared
choices.why: Right. A SUMIFS, a pivot table and a DAX measure over the same sales must agree, and when they do not, the analysis has a mistake in it.

choices.text: Because Excel can hold only one data set in a workbook
choices.why: A workbook holds as many sheets and tables as you like. The choice is about teaching, not a limit.

choices.text: So the student never needs to save a second copy of the file
choices.why: The lesson asks for exactly that second copy, to start again from.

choices.text: Because a fresh data set in every lesson would need a database server to hold it
choices.why: Each lesson could paste its own block. One business is chosen so results can be cross-checked.

prompt: Your Excel is set to Portuguese and you type `=SUMIFS(E2:E109, G2:G109, "Online")` exactly as printed. What happens?
hint: Two things change with the language, and the address is not one of them.

choices.text: It works, because function names are the same in every language
choices.why: Excel translates function names; in Portuguese this one is SOMASES.

choices.text: Excel refuses it: the name and the commas belong to the English spelling
choices.why: Right. In Portuguese the function is SOMASES and the arguments are separated by semicolons.

choices.text: It works, but the result is in a different currency
choices.why: A formula's language has nothing to do with currency.

choices.text: Excel translates the column letters to Portuguese ones
choices.why: Cell addresses never change with the language.

prompt: How were the results of the course's Power Query steps and DAX measures produced?
hint: Section 02 says which program computed what.

choices.text: By Excel for Windows, on the author's computer
choices.why: The course says plainly it was written on a computer with no Excel.

choices.text: By LibreOffice Calc, which runs Power Query
choices.why: Calc ran the formulas of lessons 1 to 12. Power Query and DAX have no engine outside Excel.

choices.text: By a script doing the same steps
choices.why: Right, and lessons 13 to 16 say so where it happens.

choices.text: They were estimated by hand and rounded
choices.why: Every number in the course was computed, never typed.

prompt: Which feature used in this course exists only in Excel for Windows?
hint: Look at the last row of the table of features.

choices.text: XLOOKUP
choices.why: Excel for Mac and Excel for the web have it too, in current versions.

choices.text: Pivot tables
choices.why: Every current Excel has them, including the web version.

choices.text: Power Pivot
choices.why: Right. Not on the Mac, not in the browser, not in any free alternative.

choices.text: Conditional formatting
choices.why: That is in every Excel and in the free alternatives.

prompt: A student has a MacBook and a Microsoft 365 subscription. What does the course recommend for lessons 15 and 16?
hint: What does a Mac lack, and how do you get it on a Mac?

choices.text: Excel for the web, which has Power Pivot in the browser
choices.why: The browser version cannot create a Power Pivot model.

choices.text: Windows in a virtual machine, with Excel for Windows inside it
choices.why: Right. It costs a Windows licence and room for a second system, and it gives every lesson.

choices.text: LibreOffice Calc from version 24.8, which added the data model
choices.why: Calc has no Power Pivot at any version.

choices.text: Skip both lessons, since a Mac covers lessons 1 to 14
choices.why: The course offers a path for them; lesson 17 also builds on what they make.

prompt: Why does the course name Excel for the web as a path and still not rely on it?
hint: Two reasons: what it lacks, and who sets its terms.

choices.text: It lacks Power Pivot, and a free tier changes on its owner's terms
choices.why: Right. It is a way to start today, not a way to finish the course.

choices.text: It needs a paid subscription that costs more than the desktop app
choices.why: A free Microsoft account opens it.

choices.text: It spells every function differently from desktop Excel, so formulas cannot be copied
choices.why: The functions are the same; some commands are missing or elsewhere.

choices.text: It runs only on Windows computers
choices.why: It runs in a browser on any system.

prompt: You type `=XLOOKUP(1,{1},{1})` and the cell shows `#NAME?`. What is the most likely cause?
hint: What does `#NAME?` say Excel did not recognise?

choices.text: The workbook has not been saved yet
choices.why: Saving has nothing to do with whether a function exists.

choices.text: This Excel is older than the function
choices.why: Right: Excel 2019 and earlier do not have XLOOKUP. Lesson 4 also teaches INDEX and MATCH for that case.

choices.text: The arguments should be separated by semicolons
choices.why: A separator problem stops Excel accepting the formula at all; it does not produce #NAME?.

choices.text: The cell is formatted as a date
choices.why: Formatting changes how a result is drawn, not whether the function is known.

prompt: After pasting the Sales block, every row sits in column A. Which fix does the lesson give?
hint: The values were meant to be split at one character.

choices.text: Format column A as Text and paste again
choices.why: The format does not split anything; the separator was lost.

choices.text: Data › Text to Columns, Delimited, with Tab ticked
choices.why: Right, or copy again with the block's button so the tabs survive.

choices.text: Turn on the Power Pivot add-in and paste again
choices.why: Power Pivot has nothing to do with pasting.

choices.text: Change the list separator of the computer to a comma
choices.why: The data is split at tabs, not at commas.

prompt: Excel for Windows shows no Power Pivot tab. Where does the lesson send you first?
hint: It ships switched off.

choices.text: File › Options › Add-ins, under COM Add-ins
choices.why: Right: tick Microsoft Power Pivot for Excel there.

choices.text: Data › Get Data › From Other Sources
choices.why: That is Power Query, a different tool.

choices.text: File › Account › Update Options
choices.why: An update does not switch an add-in on.

choices.text: Insert › PivotTable › From Data Model
choices.why: That option needs Power Pivot already working.

prompt: Put the lesson's three checks of a new Excel in the order it gives them.
hint: From what you have, to a function, to the data tools.
items: Read the version under File › Account
Type a formula that uses XLOOKUP
Look for Get Data and the Power Pivot tab
trap: Checking the tabs first tells you nothing about why a function might be missing.

prompt: On the `Sales` sheet, what does `=COUNTA(A:A)` return once the block is pasted?
hint: The sales plus one row that is not a sale.

prompt: How many bags does `=SUM(E:E)` add up on the `Sales` sheet?
hint: Run it on your own sheet.

prompt: Why does `Sales` carry its own `Price` column when `Products` already has a list price?
hint: Is what a customer paid always today's list price?

choices.text: Paid prices differ from today's list
choices.why: Right. The price of a sale is a fact about that sale.

choices.text: Because a lookup formula is not allowed to read another sheet
choices.why: Lookups read other sheets all the time; lesson 4 does it.

choices.text: Excel needs a number column in every table to build a pivot
choices.why: A pivot can count rows with no number column at all.

choices.text: It is a copy kept as a backup in case Products is deleted
choices.why: It is not a copy: in most rows it differs from the list price.

prompt: Why does the lesson ask for a second file, `cafe-serra-original.xlsx`, that you never edit?
hint: Several lessons change the data on purpose.

choices.text: Excel cannot open the same data twice without it
choices.why: Excel opens one file as often as you like.

choices.text: To start again from clean data, without pasting it all
choices.why: Right. A clean copy is cheaper than repeating the paste and the checks.

choices.text: Because Power Query reads only files that are never edited
choices.why: Power Query reads any file; the copy is for you.

choices.text: To keep the file small enough to send by e-mail
choices.why: Two files take more space, not less.

prompt: The sentence that finishes *each row is one…* names the table's ___.
hint: A word for the level of detail of a row.

prompt: If each row of `Sales` were one order, and an order could hold two products, what would go wrong?
hint: Where would the second product go?

choices.text: Nothing: the grain makes no difference to formulas
choices.why: The grain decides what one row means and so what every count counts.

choices.text: Every question about products would need to read two columns
choices.why: Right. A row of one sale keeps one product per row.

choices.text: Excel would refuse to store more than one date per row
choices.why: Excel stores whatever you type; the problem is analysis, not storage.

choices.text: The Customer column would have to move to another sheet
choices.why: An order still has one customer; the trouble is the products.

prompt: Match each column to what it is.
hint: A key identifies a row of its own table; a pointer holds another table's key.

pairs.right: The key of its own table
A pointer to a row of another table
A quantity measured on each record

right_distractors: A total kept among the data

prompt: Café Serra renames the product `CER1K`. With the three tables as given, how many cells have to change?
hint: Where is a product's name written?

choices.text: One: the product's name, in its own row of Products
choices.why: Right. Sales holds only the code, so every sale follows the new name.

choices.text: Twenty-eight, one for each sale of it
choices.why: Sales does not hold the name; that is the point of the key.

choices.text: Twenty-nine, the sales and the product row
choices.why: The sales hold the code, which does not change.

choices.text: None, because a name cannot be changed once used
choices.why: It can, and with this layout it costs one cell.

prompt: A report sheet has a subtotal row under each group. What does `=SUM` over its whole January column give?
hint: Each bag appears in more than one row.

choices.text: The right total, because Excel skips subtotal rows
choices.why: SUM adds every number in the range; it cannot tell a subtotal from a sale.

choices.text: A total that counts some bags two or three times
choices.why: Right: once in their row, again in the subtotal, and again in the grand total if it is inside the range.

choices.text: An error, because the column mixes text and numbers
choices.why: SUM ignores text and adds the numbers, which is the problem.

choices.text: Only the subtotals, because they are formulas
choices.why: SUM adds typed numbers and formula results alike.

prompt: Which of these break the one-row-per-record shape? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask of each: can a formula read it row by row?

choices.text: A blank row between 2025 and 2026
choices.why: It cuts the range in two, and tools see only the half you started in.

choices.text: `14 bags` typed in the Bags column
choices.why: The unit turns the number into text, and SUM skips it.

choices.text: A row painted yellow to mean unpaid
choices.why: No formula can count a colour. A column saying Paid would do it.

choices.text: A Date column holding a real date on every row
choices.why: That is exactly the shape: one value per cell, one field per column.

prompt: A colleague's sheet has the months January to December as columns. Next January a thirteenth month arrives. What is the cheapest correct fix?
hint: Where should a month live in a record-shaped sheet?

choices.text: Insert a column for the new month and widen every formula
choices.why: That repeats the problem every month; the formulas will be widened again next time.

choices.text: Start a new sheet for the new year with the same layout
choices.why: Now a year-on-year question has to read two sheets.

choices.text: Store the month as a value of a date column
choices.why: Right. New months are then new rows, and every formula already covers them. Lesson 14 does this with unpivot.

choices.text: Rename the January column to January and February
choices.why: Two months in one column is two values per cell.

prompt: You change Sales!B2, which shows `2025-01-02`, to the General format. What does it show?
hint: A date is a count of days.

choices.why: Right. The format drew it as a date; the value was always a number.
That is only the year, which the YEAR function would extract.

choices.text: #VALUE!
choices.why: Changing a format never produces an error.

choices.text: 2025-01-02 as text, aligned left
choices.why: The value does not become text; it is drawn as a plain number.

prompt: If S1001's 14 bags had been typed as text with an apostrophe, what would `=SUM(E:E)` on Sales return?
hint: The sum leaves the text cell out.

prompt: A cell shows `104` and a formula using it behaves as if it held 103.5. Why?
hint: What a cell shows and what it holds can differ.

choices.text: Excel rounds every number it stores to the nearest half
choices.why: Excel stores the number you gave it, to about fifteen digits.

choices.text: It holds 103.5 and is formatted with no decimals
choices.why: Right. Formulas use the stored value; ROUND is how you store what you mean.

choices.text: The formula has a typing error in it
choices.why: The formula is doing exactly what it should with the stored value.

choices.text: The number was stored as text
choices.why: Text would be skipped by arithmetic, not used as 103.5.

prompt: Match each check formula, run on the pasted data, to what it answers.
hint: Run them if you are not sure.

prompt: A file from another system is pasted and `=COUNT(E:E)` answers 0 where 108 numbers are expected, while every value looks right. What has happened?
hint: COUNT counts one kind of value.

choices.text: The numbers arrived as text, so sums over them are 0
choices.why: Right. Lesson 6 converts them back; until then no total over that column can be trusted.

choices.text: The column is formatted with no decimals
choices.why: A format does not stop a number being counted.

choices.text: The values are numbers but COUNT ignores pasted cells
choices.why: COUNT counts numbers wherever they came from.

choices.text: Column E is empty and the values are drawn by a format
choices.why: A format draws a value the cell holds; it cannot invent one.

prompt: Put the making of the workbook in order.
hint: The lesson's numbered steps.
items: Paste the first block into A1
Add Products and Customers and paste into each
Save, then save the untouched copy
trap: Saving the untouched copy before checking keeps a broken paste as your clean start.
